title: The Adi Granth installed, 1604
hook: the book is placed in the Harmandir and Baba Buddha reads the first hukam

segments.voice: Yesterday, raag, and gathering the hymns: Guru Arjan and Bhai Gurdas made one book. Your line was gather what is true.

The book is finished. Page after page, written by hand, every hymn set under its raga. Now what? You could put it on a shelf, or keep it in the Guru's own room. Guru Arjan did neither. In 1604 the book was carried in procession to the Harmandir Sahib, the house with four doors in the middle of the pool. Tradition says the old man Baba Buddha, who had known Guru Nanak as a boy, carried it on his head, and the Guru walked behind with a whisk, waving it over the book the way you'd honor a king.
screen: `THE BOOK IS FINISHED.` → `CARRIED ON BABA BUDDHA'S HEAD.` → `THE GURU WALKS BEHIND.`

segments.voice: Adi means first, or original. Granth means book. The first book: that's what Sikhs call the volume Guru Arjan compiled. Much later it would become the Guru Granth Sahib, a story for another day. Now watch what happens in the Harmandir. The book is placed on a raised seat in the center, under a canopy, and the Guru sits below it. The man who made it takes a humbler place than the words. Baba Buddha is named the first granthi, the keeper and reader of the book. Then comes a moment Sikhs still repeat each day. He opens the book at random and reads the hymn at the top of the left page. That reading is called a hukam, an order, or a word for the day. Tradition says the very first hukam was a line of Guru Arjan's own, saying in plain words that God himself stands up to carry out the work of the saints. A fitting word for a new house. The practice goes on in gurdwaras all over the world: every morning the book is opened, and a random hymn is read as the word for the day. Some Sikhs look up the Harmandir Sahib's hukam on their phones before breakfast. A practice from 1604, in your pocket. The words were gathered, sorted and guarded. Now they have a home, a keeper, and a voice.
screen: `ADI GRANTH — THE FIRST BOOK.` · `THE GURU SITS LOWER THAN THE BOOK.` · `BABA BUDDHA, THE FIRST READER.` · `A HUKAM, A WORD FOR THE DAY.` · then, large: `THE WORD HAS A HOME.`

segments.voice: Let any book near you fall open, a novel, a cookbook, a book of poems, a holy book if you have one, and read the first line your eye lands on, slowly, twice. Then close it and sit with the line, the way a room full of people sits with the day's hukam. It may mean nothing, or it may land exactly; let it be the word you were handed.
Adi Granth. The first book, compiled by Guru Arjan and installed in the Harmandir Sahib in 1604, with the Guru seated below it.
Your line: the word has a home. Tomorrow, the story turns hard. Day sixty-two, done.

howItsDone: Every day in gurdwaras, the Guru Granth Sahib is opened and a hymn read at random as the hukam, the day's word; the hukam from the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar is shared widely each morning.

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: 'hundreds of pages' cut (no count in the source); removed the stock aside 'here's the thing a curious person could repeat tonight'; 'every single day' softened.
Traditional first hukam: 'santa ke karaj aap khaloia' (Ang 783), paraphrased as God himself standing up to carry out the work of the saints. Confirm Ang and paraphrase.
Baba Buddha carrying the book on his head and Guru Arjan waving the chaur (whisk) behind is tradition; confirm.
The later title Guru Granth Sahib (1708) is only mentioned, held for a later day. Confirm.
Pronunciation 'AA-d GRUNTH' is approximate (the final short i of ਆਦਿ is barely voiced). Confirm.
